title: Japan to Test Hypersonic Missiles on Australian Ranges Under New Boobook Laser Deal; Germany Handovers Nuclear-Capable Submarine to Israel as Arms Exports Surge
subhead: Canberra and Tokyo deepen a decade-long missile-range and laser-cooperation pact, while Berlin quietly clears submarine-heavy export licences for Israel and the UK picks Tekever's AR5 drone to replace Watchkeeper.

sections.heading: Japan-Australia: Hypersonic Tests on Australian Soil and a Shared Laser Project
sections.body:
Japan and Australia's defence ministers agreed on August 18 that the Japan Self-Defence Forces will conduct test launches of standoff and hypersonic missiles on Australian ranges 'over the course of the next decade', according to Australian Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles (via AFP). Marles framed Australia as providing 'strategic depth' to Japan; his counterpart Shinjiro Koizumi called the prospect of testing hypersonic missiles in Australia 'a groundbreaking development'.

The ministers also unveiled a new co-development project named Boobook, an enhanced laser system for detecting threats that can be mounted on land combat and littoral platforms. The agreement builds on last year's A$10 billion ($6 billion), 10-year deal for Australia to acquire a fleet of Japanese-designed stealth frigates — one of Japan's largest defence exports since World War II.
sections.whyItMatters: The deal effectively expands Japan's missile test envelope and embeds Canberra-Tokyo interoperability at a time of rising Chinese military pressure in the Indo-Pacific and US demands for allies to spend more. Boobook gives both navies and armies a directed-energy counter-drone/missile capability in development.

sections.heading: Germany Hands Over Nuclear-Capable Submarine to Israel as Export Licences Surge
sections.body:
Germany approved nearly €800 million ($913 million) in arms export licences to Israel in the first five months of 2026 — more than in the previous 20 months combined — according to a Federal Foreign Office reply to a parliamentary question reported by Al Jazeera. More than 60 percent of the value is tied to a single unnamed 'major maritime project', widely identified by analysts as a TKMS-built submarine. The INS Drakon, a Dolphin II-class boat estimated at €480 million, was officially handed over to the Israeli Navy last week.

Reports suggest the Drakon may be fitted with a vertical launching system (VLS) capable of launching nuclear-tipped cruise or ballistic missiles, which would make Israel only the second navy after South Korea to field a VLS on an air-independent-propulsion conventionally powered submarine — a potential sea-based second-strike capability. Germany is reportedly financing about 30 percent of the Drakon's cost. TKMS also signed an MoU with Israel's Elbit Systems in May. Berlin's wider arms exports reached €13.87 billion in the first half of 2026, per particle.news, even as German public opinion has turned against weapons for Israel.
sections.whyItMatters: The handover sharpens Israel's strategic deterrent by adding a survivable sea-based leg, and it underscores Berlin's willingness to keep arming Israel despite Gaza-related political and legal pressures — a submarine capability no European exporter has matched for Israel.

sections.heading: UK Selects Tekever AR5 Drones to Replace Watchkeeper
sections.body:
The British Army will be equipped with Tekever AR5 surveillance drones under an investment of up to £400 million over ten years, the Ministry of Defence announced. The initial order covers six aircraft with up to 24 delivered by 2029, carrying up to 50kg of sensors. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the AR5 is 'proven in Ukraine' and was chosen to keep British troops 'ahead of emerging threats'. The aircraft will be built at Tekever's soon-to-open Swindon facility.

The AR5 replaces the Watchkeeper, a Thales UK system based on an Israeli Elbit design in service since 2014, which the MOD says is reaching the end of its operational life. Tekever is a Portuguese-founded company that already operates the AR5 under UK contract for maritime surveillance of small-boat crossings in the English Channel, and the type has seen operational use in Ukraine.
sections.whyItMatters: The contract draws a line under the Watchkeeper programme and hands the British Army a combat-proven, UK-built tactical ISR platform, while anchoring Tekever's manufacturing in Britain — a sovereign-capability and industrial-base signal in the drone space.

sections.heading: Fire Point: Ukraine's Startup Scaling Deep-Strike Missiles and Drones
sections.body:
Ukraine's leading arms company Fire Point is manufacturing about 100 Flamingo long-range cruise missiles a month, a rate the Guardian reports is enough to sustain an enduring deep-strike campaign against targets hundreds of miles inside Russia. CEO Iryna Terekh said the Flamingo, carrying 1,150kg of explosive and priced at under $600,000 per unit, flew roughly 1,800km on a June attack on a Russian components factory at Cheboksary — among the longest recorded cruise-missile mission distances. Its FP-1 and FP-2 drones, produced at 'hundreds per day', cost between $55,000 and $75,000 and have targeted Russian oil refineries, a campaign that has cut their production by around 20 percent.

Fire Point now operates from 83 factories in Ukraine plus one in Denmark, employing 6,000 people, up from 3,500 late last year (per the Guardian), with CNBC reporting the team could exceed 100,000 drones by year-end. Production is restarting after a pause tied to delays in the €90 billion EU lending package for Ukraine. Terekh told CNBC that deep strikes are a core tenet of Kyiv's pressure campaign and that it facilitates more than 60 percent of Ukraine's 'long-range sanctions'.
sections.whyItMatters: Fire Point's scale-up shows Ukraine's homegrown defence industry filling the long-range strike gap Western donors were once unwilling to provide, at unit costs far below Western cruise missiles — a model for low-cost, mass-produced deep-strike capability.

sections.heading: US Congress Backs $500 Million for Taiwan Defense While Trump Holds Arms Package
sections.body:
The US House of Representatives passed a bill including $500 million in Foreign Military Financing for Taiwan in the FY2027 appropriations package, Defense News reports, even as President Donald Trump continues to hold up a larger $14 billion weapons package he pulled back in May after meeting Chinese leader Xi Jinping. The $500 million allocation does not commit to a specific arms package, but analysts said it signals the Republican-controlled Congress still values Taiwan's defense and intends to fulfil older arms purchase deals.

'This $500 million demonstrates that Congress has not reduced its security support for Taiwan following the Trump-Xi meeting,' Huang Chung-ting of Taipei's Institute for National Defense and Security Research told Defense News. Trump's signature on the bill would imply continued weapons sales despite the fate of the $14 billion package.
sections.whyItMatters: The congressional funding keeps Taiwan's defense line alive even as the White House prioritises a Beijing thaw — a widening gap between congressional intent and executive hesitation over the island's arms supply.

sections.heading: CAE Bets on Canada's New GCAP Status to Win Fighter Work
sections.body:
Canadian simulator and defence firm CAE says it sees business opportunity in Canada's new observer status in the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), the sixth-generation fighter partnership of the UK, Japan and Italy, Breaking Defense reports. Official announcements were circumspect about an active Ottawa role in the programme, but industry officials suggest Canada's entry could open training, simulation and sustainment work for CAE and other Canadian firms.

Canada's move follows its selection of TKMS as preferred bidder to build up to 12 submarines in the largest order in the German yard's history, and sits alongside Ottawa's earlier F-35 purchase — positioning Canadian industry for a share of both Western and Pacific sixth-generation combat-air programmes.
sections.whyItMatters: Canada is threading a path into the GCAP ecosystem on an industrial, not just procurement, basis — a template for how mid-tier allies secure a foothold in sixth-generation combat-air supply chains.

bottomLine: Today's defense brief is dominated by procurement and industrial moves rather than battlefield shifts. Japan and Australia agreed a decade-long hypersonic test-and-laser cooperation pact, Germany quietly handed Israel a potentially VLS-equipped nuclear-capable submarine amid a surge in export licences, and the UK replaced Watchkeeper with Tekever's Ukraine-proven AR5. Meanwhile Ukraine's Fire Point has scaled to ~100 cruise missiles a month, the US Congress pushed $500 million toward Taiwan despite Trump's hold on a larger package, and Canada's GCAP observer status opens industrial doors for CAE. The common thread: mid-tier and non-US powers are investing in low-cost long-range strike, directed energy, and sixth-generation supply-chain positions rather than waiting on US procurement cycles.
sources: AFP via The Star, Al Jazeera, particle.news, blazetrends, UK Defence Journal, Ministry of Defence, The Guardian, CNBC, Defense News, Breaking Defense
